claim: Bending of cilia and flagella occurs when axonemal dynein molecules on one side of the axoneme produce force and move toward the microtubule (MT) minus end.
source: Bending of cilia and flagella occurs when axonemal dynein molecules on one side of the axoneme produce force and move toward the microtubule (MT) minus end.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of cilia/flagella bending based on established knowledge of axonemal dynein function.

claim: Dyneins are pulled back when the axoneme bends in the other direction, meaning oscillatory back and forth movement of dynein during repetitive bending of cilia/flagella.
source: These dyneins are then pulled back when the axoneme bends in the other direction, meaning oscillatory back and forth movement of dynein during repetitive bending of cilia/flagella.
evidence: This describes the oscillatory behavior of dyneins during ciliary/flagellar beating based on mechanical principles.

claim: Electron microscopy (EM) showed pairs of parallel MTs crossbridged by patches of regularly arranged dynein molecules bound in two different orientations.
source: Electron microscopy (EM) showed pairs of parallel MTs crossbridged by patches of regularly arranged dynein molecules bound in two different orientations, depending on which of the MTs their tails bind to.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM images shown in Figure 2A and B showing dynein molecules in two orientations.

claim: The oppositely oriented dyneins are expected to produce opposing forces when the pair of MTs have the same polarity.
source: The oppositely oriented dyneins are expected to produce opposing forces when the pair of MTs have the same polarity.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the geometry of the system and the known directionality of dynein motors.

claim: Optical trapping experiments showed that the dynein-MT-DNA-origami complex actually oscillates back and forth after photolysis of caged ATP.
source: Optical trapping experiments showed that the dynein-MT-DNA-origami complex actually oscillates back and forth after photolysis of caged ATP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and related figures showing oscillatory traces.

claim: The complex, when held at one end, showed repetitive bending motions.
source: Intriguingly, the complex, when held at one end, showed repetitive bending motions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8 and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: A simple system composed of ensembles of oppositely oriented dyneins, MTs, and inter-MT crosslinkers, without any additional regulatory structures, has an intrinsic ability to cause oscillation and repetitive bending motions.
source: The results show that a simple system composed of ensembles of oppositely oriented dyneins, MTs, and inter-MT crosslinkers, without any additional regulatory structures, has an intrinsic ability to cause oscillation and repetitive bending motions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Beating of cilia and flagella is powered by axonemal dynein molecules that are minus-end-directed microtubule (MT) motors.
source: Beating of cilia and flagella is powered by axonemal dynein molecules that are minus-end-directed microtubule (MT) motors (Gibbons and Rowe, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gibbons and Rowe, 1965.

claim: Each dynein is tethered to a doublet MT with its tail, and interacts with the neighboring MT using its stalks in an ATP-dependent way, to produce relative sliding of the two MTs.
source: Each dynein is tethered to a doublet MT with its tail, and interacts with the neighboring MT using its stalks in an ATP-dependent way, to produce relative sliding of the two MTs.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of dynein function in axonemes.

claim: The MTs in an axoneme are all parallel and arranged in a 9 + 2 structure with their minus ends at the base and interconnected with various components, such as the nexin-dynein regulatory complex.
source: The MTs in an axoneme are all parallel and arranged in a 9 + 2 structure with their minus ends at the base and interconnected with various components, such as the nexin-dynein regulatory complex (Heuser et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heuser et al., 2009 and represents established knowledge of axoneme structure.

claim: Minus-end-directed movement of the dynein molecules on one side of the axoneme causes bending of the axoneme in one direction.
source: Because the neighboring doublet MTs are interlinked and also anchored to the basal body at the base, minus-end-directed movement of the dynein molecules on one side of the axoneme causes bending of the axoneme in one direction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: During cyclical bending of the axoneme, dynein molecules oscillate back and forth along a MT.
source: Thus, during cyclical bending of the axoneme, dynein molecules oscillate back and forth along a MT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanical constraints of the axoneme structure.

claim: How a minus-end-directed motor dynein can move back and forth along a MT is unknown.
source: How a minus-end-directed motor dynein can move back and forth along a MT is unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The outer-arm dyneins are aligned in a row with a periodicity of 24 nm.
source: the outer-arm dyneins are aligned in a row with a periodicity of 24 nm, and the inner-arm dyneins are also regularly placed in specific positions (Bui et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bui et al., 2008.

claim: The inter-doublet linkers connect the circumferentially arranged nine doublet MTs, and thus transmit the force produced locally by some dyneins to the other parts of the axoneme.
source: The inter-doublet linkers connect the circumferentially arranged nine doublet MTs, and thus transmit the force produced locally by some dyneins to the other parts of the axoneme (Lindemann, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lindemann, 2003.

claim: Radial spokes and central apparatus seem to play important roles in the regulation of dynein activity.
source: Other regulatory components, such as the radial spokes and central apparatus also seem to play important roles in the regulation (Witman et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Witman et al., 1978.

claim: The high-salt-extracted dynein preparations are known to crossbridge MTs with ~24 nm periodicity.
source: The high-salt-extracted dynein preparations are known to crossbridge MTs with ~24 nm periodicity (Haimo et al., 1979)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haimo et al., 1979.

claim: Previous work showed that the proteins bound to MTs are mostly outer-arm dynein.
source: although they contain other components in addition to outer-arm dyneins, previous work showed that the proteins bound to MTs are mostly outer-arm dynein (Aoyama and Kamiya, 2010; Oda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aoyama and Kamiya, 2010 and Oda et al., 2007.

claim: The MTs became bundled with the crossbridging molecules bound with a period of ~24 nm.
source: As previously reported (Aoyama and Kamiya, 2010; Haimo et al., 1979; Oda et al., 2007), the MTs became bundled with the crossbridging molecules bound with a period of ~24 nm (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B and citations to previous work.

claim: Negative-stain EM observation of the individual crossbridges showed characteristic shapes of outer-arm dynein, with stacked heads and a tail, confirming that the crossbridging proteins are mostly outer-arm dyneins.
source: Negative-stain EM observation of the individual crossbridges showed characteristic shapes of outer-arm dynein, with stacked heads and a tail (Heuser et al., 2009; Movassagh et al., 2010; Figure 2C), confirming that the crossbridging proteins are mostly outer-arm dyneins.
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 2C and comparison with structures reported in cited literature.

claim: The average number of dyneins per 1 µm of a MT pair was about 12 when 6.25 µg/ml dynein was used.
source: The average number of dyneins per 1 µm of a MT pair was about 12 when 6.25 µg/ml dynein was used.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The majority of the Chlamydomonas-dynein-MT complexes (36 out of 44 complexes) showed parallel arrangements of the MTs as in axonemes.
source: In contrast, the majority of the Chlamydomonas-dynein-MT complexes (36 out of 44 complexes) showed parallel arrangements of the MTs as in axonemes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from EM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: In the complex with parallel MTs, the dynein molecules in two opposite orientations are expected to produce force in opposite directions.
source: In the complex with parallel MTs, the dynein molecules in two opposite orientations are expected to produce force in opposite directions (Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is an inference based on the geometry of the system and the known directionality of dynein motors.

claim: The outer-arm dynein preparations used here supported movement of MTs in gliding assays at a speed comparable to those in previous work.
source: The outer-arm dynein preparations used here supported movement of MTs in gliding assays at a speed comparable to those in previous work (Alper et al., 2013; Furuta et al., 2009; Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Many of the dynein-MT complexes showed unidirectional sliding of MTs.
source: Even though the majority of the complexes are thought to contain groups of dynein molecules that produce force in opposite directions, many of the complexes showed unidirectional sliding of MTs (Video 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 1.

claim: Some MTs slid much faster than those observed in gliding assays.
source: The velocity was variable (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1), with some MTs sliding much faster than those observed in gliding assays.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Fast sliding was previously observed with similar dynein-MT complexes but with much higher concentration of dynein, and was interpreted as the effect of cooperation of dyneins aligned with 24 nm periodicity.
source: Fast sliding was previously observed with similar dynein-MT complexes but with much higher concentration of dynein, and was interpreted as the effect of cooperation of dyneins aligned with 24 nm periodicity (Aoyama and Kamiya, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aoyama and Kamiya, 2010.

claim: Typical traces showed a maximum force of ~30 pN.
source: Typical traces showed a maximum force of ~30 pN.
evidence: This is a measurement from optical trapping experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The maximum force value is several times larger than the force produced by single molecules of outer-arm dynein from sea urchin (5–6 pN) or Tetrahymena (4.7 pN), indicating cooperative force production.
source: The value is several times larger than the force produced by single molecules of outer-arm dynein from sea urchin (5–6 pN) (Shingyoji et al., 2015) or Tetrahymena (4.7 pN) (Hirakawa et al., 2000), indicating cooperative force production.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature values, leading to an inference about cooperative behavior.

claim: Addition of enough DNA origami rods can prevent disassembly of the complex in the presence of ATP.
source: In vitro motility assays confirmed that addition of enough DNA origami rods (e.g. 2.5 nM DNA rods for the dynein-MT complex with 6.25 µg/ml dynein) can actually prevent disassembly of the complex in the presence of ATP, so that movement of MTs was not detected by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—video 1.

claim: The maximum relative sliding distance was estimated to be ~96 nm in both directions in the ideal situation where all the DNA rods are bound perpendicular to the MTs.
source: The maximum relative sliding distance was estimated to be ~96 nm in both directions in the ideal situation where all the DNA rods are bound perpendicular to the MTs.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the design of the DNA origami linkers, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DNA origami rods crosslinking the dynein-MT complex were clearly visible by EM.
source: DNA origami rods crosslinking the dynein-MT complex were clearly visible by EM (Figure 2A and B, indicated by purple arrowheads; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by EM images shown in Figure 2A, B, and D.

claim: The average number of DNA rods crosslinking a pair of MTs was ~2.4 per µm when 2.5 nM DNA rods were used.
source: The average number of DNA rods crosslinking a pair of MTs was ~2.4 per µm when 2.5 nM DNA rods were used.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: When ATP was added to the complex, the deviation of the rod angle from the perpendicular increased (p<0.002, Mann-Whitney U-test), indicating that the DNA rods tilted because of relative sliding of the MTs.
source: When ATP was added to the complex, the deviation of the rod angle from the perpendicular increased (p<0.002, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 4—source data 2), indicating that the DNA rods tilted because of relative sliding of the MTs.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—source data 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: About 48 out of 94 traces showed sliding movement, and 65% of them exhibited oscillatory movement.
source: About 48 out of 94 such traces showed sliding movement, and 65% of them exhibited oscillatory movement (at least two forward and two backward displacements, each displacement larger than 10 nm, and the velocity of each movement between 0.1 and 50 µm/s) in some parts of the trace.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the optical trapping experimental results.

claim: The amplitude of the oscillatory movements was variable, but typically within the expected maximum displacement (~96 × 2 nm), with the averages of 26.6 and 26.4 nm for the forward and backward movement, respectively.
source: The amplitude of the oscillatory movements was variable, but typically within the expected maximum displacement (~96 × 2 nm, see above), with the averages of 26.6 and 26.4 nm for the forward (away from the trap center) and backward (back toward the trap center) movement, respectively (Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The velocities of the forward and backward movements during oscillation were both in the same range as the velocity observed in the gliding assay of the dynein-MT complex without DNA rods (4.4 µm/s in average).
source: The velocities of the forward and backward movements during oscillation were also variable (Figure 6A and D and Figure 6—source data 1), but they were both in the same range as the velocity observed in the gliding assay of the dynein-MT complex without DNA rods (Figure 3B; 4.4 µm/s in average).
evidence: This is a comparison of velocities measured in different experimental conditions.

claim: The average time required for the forward and backward movements (10.1 and 8.3 ms, respectively) was substantially longer than the time required for simple detachment from a MT, which was usually less than 1 ms.
source: However, the average time required for the forward and backward movements (10.1 and 8.3 ms, respectively; Figure 6A and C and Figure 6—source data 1) was substantially longer than the time required for simple detachment from a MT, which was usually less than 1 ms.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of timescales from the experimental data.

claim: The frequencies of the oscillation were variable, with an average of 32.9 Hz.
source: The frequencies were variable, with an average of 32.9 Hz (Figure 6E, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The peaks of the step sizes were close to 8 nm (6.2, 8.4, and 9.5 nm for unidirectional movement, forward, and backward displacements of the oscillatory movement, respectively).
source: Although many of the traces of our dynein-MT-DNA-origami complex were noisy and we could not accurately measure the step sizes, the peaks of the step sizes were close to 8 nm (6.2, 8.4, and 9.5 nm for unidirectional movement, forward, and backward displacements of the oscillatory movement, respectively; Figure 6F, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from step-finding analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Both forward and backward displacements during the oscillatory movement are steps of dynein.
source: If the oscillatory movements we observed are simply the cycles of unidirectional movement and dissociation of dyneins, we would not detect multiple steps during the backward movements. Thus, the results indicate that both forward and backward displacements during the oscillatory movement are steps of dynein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the step-finding analysis of the experimental data.

claim: An ensemble of multiple uniformly oriented dynein molecules moves a MT unidirectionally.
source: Optical trapping experiments also showed at a higher resolution that the movement was unidirectional (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2), clearly different from the traces observed with the complex containing oppositely oriented dyneins (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Thus, we conclude that an ensemble of multiple uniformly oriented dynein molecules moves a MT unidirectionally, and that two groups of oppositely oriented dyneins are required for oscillation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 7B and comparison with other experimental conditions.

claim: Two groups of oppositely oriented dyneins are required for oscillation.
source: Thus, we conclude that an ensemble of multiple uniformly oriented dynein molecules moves a MT unidirectionally, and that two groups of oppositely oriented dyneins are required for oscillation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of experimental results with different dynein orientations.

claim: Increase of the length was detected for both orientations of dyneins in the presence of ATP (p<0.00001, T-test), suggesting that their structures are different from the rigor structure.
source: Although the apparent length measured in 2D images is thought to be affected by the viewing angle so that the measured values are not precise, increase of the length was detected for both orientations of dyneins in the presence of ATP (p<0.00001, T-test), suggesting that their structures are different from the rigor structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of EM measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Repetitive bending motions were observed when the dynein-MT-DNA-origami complex was held at one point.
source: Although our fluorescence microscopy setup did not allow us to detect high-frequency oscillations, repetitive bending motions were indeed observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8 and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: The complex can bend in both directions compared to the position before ATP release.
source: The plot in Figure 8B shows that the complex can bend in both directions compared to the position before ATP release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: It is likely that the bending motions in the opposite directions are powered by oppositely oriented dyneins, not just the cycles of force production and detachment.
source: Thus, it is likely that the bending motions in the opposite directions are powered by oppositely oriented dyneins, not just the cycles of force production and detachment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of bidirectional bending motions.

claim: Relative sliding distances of the MTs were estimated to be approximately 130 and 370 nm for specific frames.
source: Using these regions, relative sliding distances of the MTs were estimated to be approximately 130 and 370 nm for the frames #38 of Figure 8A and #13 of Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, respectively.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sliding distances longer than the expected maximum value (~190 nm) are thought to be caused by rearrangement of the DNA origami during MT sliding.
source: Sliding distances longer than the expected maximum value (~190 nm; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1) are thought to be caused by rearrangement of the DNA origami during MT sliding.
evidence: This is an inference to explain observations that exceed the theoretical maximum.

claim: A system composed of MTs, oppositely oriented dyneins, and inter-MT crosslinkers has the ability to bend repetitively.
source: Nevertheless, the bending motions observed here indicate that a system composed of MTs, oppositely oriented dyneins, and inter-MT crosslinkers has the ability to bend repetitively.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations of bending motions.

claim: Previous work using frayed Chlamydomonas flagella axonemes showed that a pair of doublet MTs can display cyclic association, buckling, and dissociation.
source: Previous work using frayed Chlamydomonas flagella axonemes showed that a pair of doublet MTs can display cyclic association, buckling, and dissociation (Aoyama and Kamiya, 2005; Brokaw, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aoyama and Kamiya, 2005 and Brokaw, 2009.

claim: Oscillatory movements of MTs were observed by Shingyoji et al., 1998; Shingyoji et al., 2015, using single or a few molecules of sea urchin axonemal dynein.
source: Oscillatory movements of MTs were also observed by Shingyoji et al., 1998; Shingyoji et al., 2015, using single or a few molecules of sea urchin axonemal dynein.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shingyoji et al., 1998 and Shingyoji et al., 2015.

claim: Multiple molecules of Chlamydomonas outer-arm dynein move a MT unidirectionally.
source: In contrast, our work shows that multiple molecules of Chlamydomonas outer-arm dynein move a MT unidirectionally.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the current study.

claim: The discrepancy between single molecule and ensemble behavior is caused by the number and the arrangement of molecules.
source: We think the discrepancy is caused by the number and the arrangement of molecules: our system has multiple dynein molecules (~35 on average in the case of the complex with oppositely oriented dyneins) aligned regularly on a MT, which would work cooperatively as in cilia and flagella.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the difference between the current results and previous work.

claim: Radial spokes and central apparatus are thought to be important for beating of flagella, but mutant flagella lacking radial spokes or the central pair can beat under certain conditions.
source: For example, radial spokes and central apparatus are thought to be important for beating of flagella, but mutant flagella lacking radial spokes or the central pair can beat under certain conditions (Frey et al., 1997; Yagi and Kamiya, 2000), indicating that they are not absolutely needed for oscillatory beating.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frey et al., 1997 and Yagi and Kamiya, 2000.

claim: Some modeling studies predicted that a system composed of dynein, MTs, and passive components can produce oscillation due to mechanical instability.
source: Some modeling studies predicted that a system composed of dynein, MTs, and passive components can produce oscillation due to mechanical instability (Bayly and Dutcher, 2016), but direct evidence has not been obtained because of the lack of a reconstituted system with minimal components.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bayly and Dutcher, 2016.

claim: Oscillation of this system shows that the regulatory components including the 9 + 2 structure with radial spokes and the central apparatus, nexin-dynein regulatory complexes, and inner-arm dyneins are not essential for generation of oscillation per se.
source: Oscillation of this system shows that the regulatory components including the 9 + 2 structure with radial spokes and the central apparatus, nexin-dynein regulatory complexes, and inner-arm dyneins are not essential for generation of oscillation per se.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental demonstration of oscillation in a minimal system.

claim: The most likely explanation for the oscillatory movements would be that each of the two dynein orientation-groups is responsible for just one of the two directions of movement.
source: Since our dynein-MT-DNA-origami complex contained dyneins that produce forces in opposite directions, the most likely explanation for the oscillatory movements would be that each of the two dynein orientation-groups is responsible for just one of the two directions of movement, one orientation powering forward movements and the other orientation driving backward movements (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and the geometry of the system.

claim: The average frequency of the observed oscillation (~33 Hz) was close to the beat frequencies of the two flagella of a detergent-extracted Chlamydomonas cell (30 and 45 Hz).
source: The average frequency of the observed oscillation (~33 Hz) was close to the beat frequencies of the two flagella of a detergent-extracted Chlamydomonas cell (30 and 45 Hz) (Kamiya and Hasegawa, 1987).
evidence: This is a comparison with values from cited literature.

claim: Regulatory components including the radial spokes and central apparatus are probably needed for more coordinated and long-lasting oscillation.
source: Although regulatory components including the radial spokes and central apparatus are probably needed for more coordinated and long-lasting oscillation, our results show that a minimal system composed of two groups of oppositely oriented dyneins, MTs, and inter-MT crosslinkers has an intrinsic ability to oscillate and bend cyclically.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of regulatory components based on the current findings.

claim: The dynein-MT-DNA-origami complex contains multiple dynein molecules aligned between the MTs with a 24 nm periodicity as in axonemes, allowing the neighboring dyneins to cooperate.
source: The dynein-MT-DNA-origami complex developed here contains multiple dynein molecules aligned between the MTs with a 24 nm periodicity as in axonemes, allowing the neighboring dyneins to cooperate, and the oppositely oriented dyneins to work against each other.
evidence: This is a description of the system based on EM observations.

claim: This simple system is useful for future research on the mechanism of cilia/flagella motility.
source: This simple system is thus useful for future research on the mechanism of cilia/flagella motility.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of the system for future research.

claim: The system can be used to study the high-resolution structures of dynein during oscillatory movement.
source: It can also be used to study the high-resolution structures of dynein during oscillatory movement.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential application of the system for structural studies.
